title: CHAPTER 8: BLOOD, CIRCULATORY AND LYMPHATIC SYSTEM

blocks.content: 1. Circulatory System – Introduction

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Blood consists of liquid plasma (55%) and formed elements (45%) comprising RBCs, WBCs, and platelets.
Red Blood Cells (Erythrocytes) lack a nucleus in mature human cells and carry oxygen via hemoglobin with a 120-day lifespan.
White Blood Cells (Leukocytes) function in body defense, divided into granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes).
The human heart is four-chambered and drives double circulation involving systemic and pulmonary circuits.
The lymphatic system collects excess interstitial tissue fluid (lymph) and returns it to the circulatory system while providing immune defense.

blocks.content:
The circulatory system is responsible for the transport of substances throughout the body.

It carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste products from one part of the body to another.

The circulatory system maintains internal balance and helps in regulation of body temperature.

In humans, the circulatory system is a closed type of system.

It works in coordination with respiratory, digestive, and excretory systems.
2. Components of Circulatory System

The circulatory system consists of three main components: heart, blood, and blood vessels.

The heart acts as a pumping organ.

Blood is the fluid connective tissue.

Blood vessels form a network of tubes.

These components together ensure proper circulation of blood throughout the body.
3. Blood – Definition and Functions

Blood is a fluid connective tissue that circulates throughout the body.

It transports oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, hormones, and waste materials.

Blood helps in regulation of body temperature.

It plays an important role in immunity.

Blood also helps in clotting to prevent blood loss.
4. Composition of Blood

Blood consists of plasma and formed elements.

Plasma is the liquid part of blood.

Formed elements include red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

Plasma contains water, proteins, salts, nutrients, and hormones.

Formed elements perform specific functions.
5. Red Blood Cells (RBCs)

Red blood cells are also called erythrocytes.

They contain hemoglobin which helps in transport of oxygen.

RBCs are biconcave in shape.

In humans, RBCs do not have a nucleus.

The lifespan of RBCs is about 120 days.

They are formed in bone marrow.

6. White Blood Cells (WBCs)

White blood cells are also called leukocytes.

They protect the body against infections.

WBCs are nucleated cells.

They are of two main types: granulocytes and agranulocytes.

WBCs play an important role in immunity.
7. Platelets

Platelets are also called thrombocytes.

They help in blood clotting.

Platelets prevent excessive blood loss during injury.

They are produced in bone marrow.

Their lifespan is about 7–10 days.
8. Blood Groups

Blood groups are determined by the presence or absence of antigens.

The ABO blood group system was discovered by Karl Landsteiner.

The four main blood groups are A, B, AB, and O.

Rh factor determines positive and negative blood groups.

Blood transfusion must be done carefully to avoid reactions.

blocks.content: 9. Heart – Structure

The heart is a muscular organ located in the chest cavity.

It is protected by ribs and sternum.

The heart is divided into four chambers: two atria and two ventricles.

The heart pumps blood throughout the body.

Valves prevent backflow of blood.
10. Working of Heart

The heart works continuously to circulate blood.

The right side of heart pumps deoxygenated blood to lungs.

The left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body.

This circulation is known as double circulation.

Double circulation ensures efficient oxygen supply.
11. Blood Vessels

Blood vessels are of three types: arteries, veins, and capillaries.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

Veins carry blood towards the heart.

Capillaries connect arteries and veins.

Capillaries allow exchange of materials.
12. Lymphatic System – Introduction

The lymphatic system consists of lymph, lymph vessels, and lymph nodes.

Lymph is a colorless fluid.

It helps in removal of waste products.

The lymphatic system plays an important role in immunity.

It maintains fluid balance in the body.

items: Karl Landsteiner discovered ABO blood groups; O negative is the universal donor and AB positive is the universal acceptor.
The SA Node (Sinoatrial Node) in the right atrium acts as the natural pacemaker of the human heart.
Normal human blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg (Systolic/Diastolic), measured using a Sphygmomanometer.
Erythroblastosis Fetalis occurs due to Rh incompatibility when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus.

blocks.content: 13. Lymph

Lymph is a fluid connective tissue.

It lacks RBCs but contains WBCs.

Lymph transports absorbed fats from intestine.

It returns tissue fluid back to blood.

Lymph helps in defense against infections.
14. Disorders of Circulatory System

Several disorders affect the circulatory system.

Anemia occurs due to deficiency of hemoglobin.

Leukemia is cancer of blood cells.

Hypertension is high blood pressure.

Heart attack occurs due to blockage of coronary arteries.
15. IMPORTANT FACTS –  FOCUS

• Blood is a connective tissue.

• RBCs contain hemoglobin.

• Lifespan of RBC is 120 days.

• Platelets help in clotting.

• ABO blood group was discovered by Karl Landsteiner.

• Heart has four chambers.

• Humans have double circulation.

• Arteries carry blood away from heart.

• Lymph lacks RBCs.

• Anemia is caused by hemoglobin deficiency.
